# The POPL 2019 paper against the judgement: what changes

## In short

- The paper confirms the large calls: the exclusion rule kept, the tower flat, the 2009 overload sentence gone, the three rules, the return-type rule in the form batch 7b's rung C plans, applicability and specificity on declared quantified domains, and the implicit bound `Any`.
- It contradicts one default and one mechanism, both in batches not yet run or cheap to change: item 30's "least instance" is the 2012 rule the paper says the team could not prove and abandoned; the checker's binding of an unconstrained type parameter to `Bottom` (rows 447, 425, 516) is what the paper's model forbids outright. The paper's rule for both is the same sentence: instantiate at the intersection of the upper bounds, the declared bound and the call's static return type, never at the value's type alone and never at `Bottom`.
- It adds four things the record lacked: that rule; the exact form of the overloading rules with "existential reduction"; a restriction that its proof needs (a method type parameter may not appear in another's upper bound), which the library's `SUM`, `BIG MAX` and `Integral` families break; and a phase-5 requirement, that the dispatcher must know the call's static return type at run time.
- Three things should be done differently, all cheap: item 30's sentence in 7b's rung S and one test pair in rung C; the `Bottom` binding replaced by the bound in one checker rung, which replaces the "treat as a throw" fix the judgement recommended for row 447; row 516's union replaced by the bound. Nothing on route A, answer 9, item 26 or the conversion order changes.

## 0. What the record knew, and what the paper says

The record's account (`literature.md` § 1) was right as far as it went: the paper keeps the invariant-instantiation exclusion through its ancestor rule, moves the return-type check to run time, and has no self types and no numeric tower. What it did not have, each checked in the text:

- The instance rule. "The Fortress team had assumed, because it seemed from several working examples to be in accord with intuition, that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type parameter have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower bounds should be chosen as the type to be used for that type parameter. We considered this and the hybrid technique ... but we were unable to complete the proofs of correctness of both the techniques. Since the minimum requirement for a type to instantiate a method type parameter is that it satisfies all the lower and upper bounds of the type parameter, the dynamic dispatch algorithm presented here always chooses the intersection of the upper bounds." (§ 5.4, p. 11:25, lines 1274-1284.) The rule itself is [Solve-Step] (§ 5.2.3, p. 11:19, lines 965-1016): the substitution for a parameter is the intersection of its computed upper bound and its declared upper bounds, checked against the lower bounds; "Because g' is a ground type, the solving step never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom."
- The static return type at run time. Dispatch "seeks the most specific method declaration with a dispatchable instance that is applicable to the ilk of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the annotated static return type" ([R-Method], § 5.2.1, p. 11:17, lines 888-896); "the language semantics needs to make the static types of method invocations available at run time" (§ 2.3, p. 11:7, lines 329-331). The upper bound of a return-only parameter comes from that static return type ([Dispatch], line 875: `g match ρ - bounds`).
- The default bound. "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom" (§ 3.2, p. 11:9, lines 418-419). `Bottom` "is intentionally not expressible in the surface syntax" (line 438).
- The overloading rules in checkable form (§ 4, Figure 5, p. 11:13, lines 630-661): No Duplicates as non-subtyping of domains either way; Meet as exclusion, subtyping or a third declaration whose domain is equivalent to the intersection ([Meet-Third], line 645); Return Type as one universal subtyping check, `arrow(d1) ⊑ ∀[κ,κ']((α ⊓ α') → ρ')` ([Return-Test], lines 656-660). Specificity is subtyping of existentially quantified domains, "a sound approximation of the subset relation of applicable sets, [but] not complete" (§ 4.2, p. 11:13, lines 673-675), narrowed by "existential reduction", which collects the constraints that keep a domain off `Bottom` and solves them (lines 733-743, Figure 6).
- A restriction the proof needs. A method's type parameter bindings are well formed only if "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" and every reference falls within a left-to-right scope; "restriction (1) makes dynamic dispatch more efficient and restriction (2) makes it consistent" (§ 3.3, p. 11:11, lines 565-570); the one-pass right-to-left solve depends on it (lines 1010-1016, 1258-1262). Trait type parameters carry no such restriction.
- What the calculus leaves out. "FGFV omits functional methods [Allen et al. 2007] and declarations of closed types [Allen et al. 2011], but these could be added back to FGFV in an obvious way" (§ 1, p. 11:3, lines 142-144); "FGFV does not support features like modularity, nominal exclusion, and closed types in their work, [but] they can be added in an obvious way" (§ 6, p. 11:25, lines 1302-1303). No coercion, no `nat` parameters, no numbers.
- The exclusion rule's form and date. [Anc-Same-Trait] (Figure 4, p. 11:11, lines 530-532): a class extending two instances of a trait must extend an instance below both; "the 'Ancestor Meet Rule' ... was introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase" (§ 5.4, p. 11:24, lines 1230-1232). For an invariant parameter only the same instance is below both; for a covariant one the lower instance is.
- Variance in full: marks `+ - =` on trait parameters, objects always invariant (§ 3.2, lines 406-409); a covariant parameter only in covariant positions, a contravariant one only in contravariant ones ([D-Method], § 3.3, pp. 11:11-12, lines 571-595); dispatch with variance marks (§ 5.2.2); exponential blowup only where union types meet contravariance, accepted (§ 5.4, lines 1239-1257); the two alternatives the team weighed in 2012, dropping contravariance or dropping union types.
- Cost. "In simple invariant cases, we expect the run-time cost to be relatively low but nonzero"; for variant cases "caching or dynamic recompilation" (§ 5.4, pp. 11:24-25, lines 1263-1273).

## 1. The verdicts the paper bears on

### 1.1 Route A: the exclusion rule kept, the tower flattened (D4)

- The paper confirms the rule and the flattening. [Anc-Same-Trait] is the exclusion in the paper's own terms, and "because the rules guarantee that there always exists a single minimal ancestor when a class extends multiple instances of a trait, no ambiguous method calls are possible due to multiple instances of a trait" (p. 11:11, lines 550-554). There is no tower, no self type and no `comprises T` in it (searched).
- It adds one thing the route-C notes could not know: variance cannot rescue the tower. The self-typed algebra traits put their parameter in a parameter position (`opr =(self, other: T)`), and [D-Method] forbids a covariant parameter there (lines 571-572, 584-592). So `Equality[\+T\]` is ill formed, and the covariant clause of the ancestor rule, the only clause that admits two instances on one chain, is closed to the tower. The patents' forest rule stays what the record called it, a sketch outside the group's proven model.
- Nothing to do differently. One line for batch 7b's rung S: Appendix I's instantiation-exclusion entry cites [Anc-Same-Trait] beside the 2011 paper and the 2012 Types chapter.

### 1.2 Answer 9: the overload sentence goes, the three rules, the return-type rule over every instance (D17)

- The paper confirms the drop and the rules: a generic declaration "is applicable to a type α if there exists an instance D of d that is applicable to α" (§ 2.2, p. 11:5, lines 246-248); "we use the subtype relation of their domain types as in Allen et al. [2011]" (§ 4.1, line 604); the three rules as Figure 5 states them.
- It confirms rung C's planned form of the return-type rule. The record plans "the paper's special arrow, `∀[Δ1, Δ2] (S1 ∩ S2) → T2`, with the less specific declaration's parameters kept quantified except where the domain reduction forces an equality" (`reviews/overloading-judgement.md:93`); that is [Return-Test] with the paper's reduction in a narrower form.
- It adds the general form of that reduction (§ 4.2, lines 733-743, with the `ArrayList`/`List` example at lines 676-683 and 731-732): collect the constraints that keep the intersected domain off `Bottom`, solve them, and compare the reduced domain. The record's reduction forces equalities through instantiation exclusion only; the paper's also carries bounds it cannot solve as constraints. The difference is a family of valid overloads the revival's checker will refuse and the paper's accepts.
- Do differently: nothing in the decision. Rung C's decision record names the paper's reduction as the general form and its own as the special case; rung C's tests add the paper's `ArrayList`/`List` triple as a program, expected to be refused today and gated as an expected failure if it is. Cost: one paragraph and one test in a rung already in batch 7b.

### 1.3 The positional rule (answer 9's revival addition)

- The paper has no such rule. Type parameters are α-renamed ("We assume the conventional α-conversion to rename bound variables", line 669) and a dispatched declaration is instantiated by substitution from the ilks and the static return type ([Dispatch], line 874-879), never handed the call's written static arguments by position. So an override that reorders its parameters is well formed in the paper's model.
- The positional rule exists because the team's code generator passes written static arguments by position to whichever declaration dispatch reaches (row 398). It guards an implementation habit, not a rule of the designers' model. It refuses nothing in the library (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-7.md:234`).
- Do differently: keep the guard, since the code generator still has the habit, but batch 7b's rung S states it in a callout as a restriction of the compiled implementation pending run-time instantiation by substitution, with the paper cited, not as a rule of the language; phase 5 lifts it when the dispatcher instantiates as [Dispatch] does. Cost: wording in an entry rung S already writes.

### 1.4 The conversion-and-overloading decision of 2026-09-28 (D25, decision 1)

- The paper has no coercion, so it is silent on the order "convert only when nothing fits". It confirms the two halves the decision rests on: applicability when some instance fits (line 246-248) and specificity on declared, quantified domains (line 604, Figure 6).
- It adds a caution about what its proof covers. Its well-formedness rule (2), "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" (lines 565-570), excludes every F-bounded generic function: the library's `SUM[\T extends AdditiveGroup[\T\]\]` and `PROD` of answer 7, its `BIG MAX[\T extends StandardMax[\T\]\]`, and every function over `T extends Integral[\T\]`. The record's option-2 soundness note already found that the readings part exactly at the F-bounded shapes (`reviews/option-2-soundness.md:14`, `:54`, `:110`). So the paper's Theorem 5.11 does not cover the library's reductions, and the record should not cite it as covering them. Where such a parameter is fixed by an invariant argument type (`Generator[\T\]`), the bound is checked and never solved, which is why both the team's checker and the revival's handle it; the paper's restriction protects its one-pass solve, not those calls.
- Do differently: nothing built. The decision records of rungs S and C say in one sentence that the paper's soundness result excludes F-bounded method type parameters and closed types, and that the library's reductions rest on the 2011 rules as implemented, not on the 2019 proof.

### 1.5 Item 26: `comprises` read at the level of values, with run-time uniqueness (D27)

- The paper omits closed types and nominal exclusion and says both "can be added in an obvious way" (lines 142-144, 1302-1303). So it neither confirms nor contradicts the coverage reading, the Meet Rule's closed-trait case or row 492's repair.
- It adds one fact for the proof appendix. Theorem 4.1 (§ 4.3, p. 11:15, lines 782-789) keeps static uniqueness: No Duplicates makes the more-specific relation antisymmetric, Meet makes every applicable set a meet semilattice, and "there always exists a unique most specific method declaration". The revival's addendum gives static uniqueness up for run-time uniqueness at a call whose argument's static type sits between two closed traits (`reviews/comprises-type-level-proof-addendum.md:8-9`, `:115-116`). In the paper's model the same case would be met by the team's own plan of 2009, identifying the intersection of two closed traits with the union of their common subtypes (`Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/future.tex:285`), under which [Meet-Third] holds with a single meet and Theorem 4.1 stands. Item 26's judgement did not weigh the paper on this (searched: no citation).
- Do differently: no change to batch 7b; this is the one place the revival's type theory steps outside the designers' last proven model, and it should be said. Rung S's entry for the proof appendix says in one sentence that FGFV keeps static uniqueness as a theorem, that the coverage case is beyond FGFV, and that the revival gives up static uniqueness there on the addendum's premises. Cost: one sentence.

### 1.6 Item 30: a generic declaration beside a plain one at run time (D28)

- The paper contradicts the default and gives the rule. The record chose "the instance the value fixes, the least instance where it fixes none", Welterweight's rule (`Papers/Welterweight/dispatch.tick:189-192`: "l_j is the type inferred for P_j", the lower bound), and recorded Naden's return-type restriction as future work, weighing Naden's 2012 objection that programmers could not follow execution without static types (`literature.md` § 1). The paper, with Steele among its authors, took the other road: static return types are carried to run time ([R-Method], lines 888-896), and the instance is the intersection of the upper bounds, the declared bound and the static return type's constraint, never the lower bound alone (lines 1274-1284). It says in so many words that the lower-bound rule could not be proven.
- Where the two rules agree: a parameter fixed by an invariant position in a parameter type (`grab[\X\](t: Tag[\X\])`), since lower and upper bound coincide, which is the case the judgement's example and rung W's row 157 concern. Where they differ: a parameter that is the whole type of a parameter or occurs only covariantly. `id[\T\](x: T): Box[\T\]` called through `r: Any = id(z)` with a `ZZ32` value gives `Box[\ZZ32\]` under the record's rule and `Box[\Any\]` under the paper's; a later dispatch on the box tells them apart.
- Where they meet answer 8: the revival's static promotion instantiates `op[\T extends Number\](z, w)` at `ZZ64` and annotates the call's result `ZZ64`; the paper's run-time rule then gives `Number ⊓ ZZ64 = ZZ64`, the same instance. So the paper's rule reproduces rung I's static choice at run time from the annotation, which the "least instance" rule does not promise.
- Walk cannot apply the paper's rule: it has no static types, so no static return type to constrain the instance; the value's type is all it has. That is walk's limit, as for coercion (judgement, item 7).
- Do differently, in batch 7b: rung S states the paper's rule as the designers' latest word in the dispatch paragraph (the dispatched declaration's parameters instantiated at the intersection of their upper bounds under the call's static return type, never `Bottom`), and states in a callout that both implementations today take the value's type where nothing fixes the parameter, walk by necessity and the compiled path until phase 5. Rung C adds one expected-failure pair for the case where the two rules differ (the `Box[\Any\]` shape above) beside the two it already adds. Rung W's row-157 fix stays, being walk's best. Phase 5's list gains one line: the dispatcher needs the call's static return type, which the team's code generator does not pass (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:2048`, "Not sure what to do with return type"). Cost: wording in a rung that already edits the passage, one test pair, one plan line.

### 1.7 The implicit bound `Any` (Q1; the judgement's item 3)

- The paper confirms it: "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom" (lines 418-419). The judgement's item 3 stands with this as its deciding citation; rung S cites it in the callout that revises `trait-parameters.tex:49-50`. Nothing else changes.

### 1.8 Row 447, the written `extends Object` bound, and every `Bottom` binding (D23 decision 2; the judgement's commission error 1 and item 2)

- The paper contradicts the mechanism and gives the fix. Its type system "requires that both static and dynamic type inference algorithms instantiate type parameters with non-Bottom types" (lines 845-847, 884, 1119-1120), the solving step "never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom" (lines 1005-1006), and an otherwise unconstrained parameter takes the intersection of its upper bounds: its declared bound, `Any` by default, and the static return type's constraint.
- Under that rule the crashes of row 447 do not arise. `fail[\T\]("...")` in a `ZZ32` value position is instantiated at `ZZ32`; `r: Any = et(z)` instantiates `et` at `Any`, and `BoxT[\Any\]` is a class that exists, where `BoxT[\Bottom\]` carried as `java/lang/Object` was not. The compiled checker's solver does the opposite today: an inference variable left open is bound to `BOTTOM` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/useful/STypesUtil.scala:1954-1955`, `killIvars`; `Formula.scala:524`), which is why rung B's written bound "works" and why the kept expected type of rung I still binds `Bottom` (row 447's later notes). The Working Draft's own note asks "Do we want to forbid such cases where type inference infers BottomTypes for static parameters?" (`Specification/basic/inference.tex:233-234`); the paper is the designers' answer.
- This replaces the judgement's item 2. Treating a `Bottom`-typed call as a `throw` in the code generator was a repair of the symptom; the paper's rule removes the cause and is the designers' own, and it reaches row 425 (a generic big operator's no-argument form bound to `Bottom`), the interpreter's counterpart row 424 (walk erases an unwritten static argument to `Bottom`; it should take the bound), and the inference chapter's callout (`inference.tex:212-215`), which today describes the `Bottom` binding as the checker's behaviour.
- Do differently: one checker rung, in batch 8 or beside rung Q in batch N's second run, that binds an inference variable with no lower bound to the intersection of its upper bounds instead of `BOTTOM`, with row 447's two probes and row 425's `SUM[j <- lo#i] (3 j)` as its tests (row 425 may need the big-operator desugaring's bounds as well; the rung measures it); rung B's written `extends Object` lines become unnecessary and may stay; one walk rung for row 424 later. The inference chapter's callout and its Appendix I entry change in the same batch. Cost: two small rungs; it removes a phase-4 prerequisite the judgement had ranked first among the errors of commission.

### 1.9 Row 516: a lone type parameter with no narrowest candidate (D23 decision 3, batch N's chapter)

- The paper contradicts the chapter's rule. The chapter gives such a parameter "the union of the types of those arguments" (`inference.tex:95-98`); the paper says that is the assumption the team could not prove, and takes the intersection of the upper bounds, the declared bound or `Any`. Both implementations already take the bound where one is written (row 516: `pick[\T extends Number\](w, r)` is a `BoxT[\Number\]` on both paths), and the two expected-failure tests `XXXInferLoneBoundUnion` and `XXXInferLoneUnionWalk` pin the union as the intended behaviour.
- Answer 8's promotion is not touched: it is a coercion the paper does not model, and for number arguments it decides the instance statically before the paper's rule applies (1.6 above).
- Do differently: batch 7b's rung S, whose file list already gains the inference chapter, replaces the union sentence by the bound (the declared bound, `Any` if none, under the static return type), citing the paper; the two expected-failure tests become plain tests of the bound behaviour; the checker's union candidate for an unbounded parameter (`Functionals.scala:334-343`, the `named` list, and the union fallback planned for rows 515 and 518) becomes `Any`. Cost: one sentence, two test flips, a few checker lines in the rung of 1.8. Nothing fast is lost: a body at the union of two unrelated types is a body at `Any` in the generated code.

### 1.10 The `covariant` keyword (row 404; answer 6's road back)

- The paper confirms the direction and is the specification for it: the marks, the position check, the ancestor rule under variance, dispatch with marks, and the cost. It also confirms answer 6's road back: phantom covariant parameters appear in no position, so they pass [D-Method] trivially.
- Nothing to do now; it is off the path. Row 404 and worklist item 12 point to the paper as their design when they are built.

### 1.11 Walk's run-time choice of coercions (the judgement's item 7)

- The paper is silent on coercion. But its whole dynamic semantics needs the static types of invocations at run time (lines 329-331, 820-824), which walk does not have. So walk cannot implement the designers' last model of dispatch either, and the judgement's reading, walk's run-time choice accepted as the interpreter's limit and the compiled path following the text, is strengthened. Nothing changes; the road to a walk that matches is static types under walk, his wish of 2026-09-15.

### 1.12 The omissions the judgement named

- Phase 4's natives, the sized model, decision A's store, the algebra bounds: the paper has no library, no `nat` parameters, no unboxing; silent.
- One addition to phase 5's list, from 1.6 and 1.8: the compiled dispatcher must receive the call's static return type. Without it the paper's instance rule cannot be applied at run time, and the return-type check that makes generic-beside-plain sound under variance is unavailable. The team's code generator does not pass it.
- One addition to phase 6's, from § 5.4: the paper expects run-time instantiation to cost "relatively low but nonzero" in the invariant case and names caching and dynamic recompilation for the variant ones (lines 1263-1273). MicroGPT's generics are invariant.

### 1.13 Row 508 and the attempt order (the judgement's item 4)

- Silent: no coercion in the paper. Item 4 stands as written.

## 2. Verdicts the paper leaves untouched, by name

F1, F2, F3 (its ranking of texts is confirmed, not changed), D1, D2, D3, D5, D6 (rows 329 and 330), D7, D8, D9, D10, D11, D12, D13, D14, D15, D16, D18, D19, D20 (sizes; the paper has none), D21, D22, D23's decisions 1, 4 and 5, D24, D25's decision 2, D26, D29, and the judgement's items 1, 4, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10 and 11.

## 3. What to do differently, by batch and cost

1. Batch 7b, rung S (not yet run): item 30's dispatch sentence states the paper's instance rule, with today's "value's type" behaviour in a callout (1.6); the positional rule labelled an implementation restriction (1.3); the implicit bound's callout cites the paper (1.7); row 516's union sentence replaced by the bound (1.9); one sentence each on static uniqueness in the proof-appendix entry (1.5), on the paper's exclusions in the overloading entry (1.4), and [Anc-Same-Trait] in the exclusion entry (1.1). All in files rung S already edits. Cost: wording.
2. Batch 7b, rung C: one expected-failure pair for the instance rule (1.6); the paper's `ArrayList`/`List` triple as a test (1.2). Cost: two tests.
3. Batch 8, or batch N's second run beside rung Q: one checker rung replacing the `BOTTOM` binding by the intersection of the upper bounds, tests from rows 447 and 425, the union candidate replaced by `Any` (1.8, 1.9). Cost: one small rung. It retires the judgement's item 2 and its "before phase 4" prerequisite.
4. Later: one walk rung for row 424 (the bound, not `Bottom`) (1.8); a phase-5 line for the static return type at dispatch (1.12); row 404 pointed at the paper (1.10).

## For Pavol

The question in one line: does the full POPL 2019 paper, the type group's last published word, say anything that means we should do something differently?

What changes:

- Three things, all cheap, none built yet. First, the answer you gave on item 30 (2026-09-29, "only option one makes sense") took the 2012 rule, the instance the value fixes. The 2019 paper says the team could not prove that rule and replaced it: the instance is fixed by the declared bound and by the call's static result type, never by the value alone. For microGPT the two agree, because its static types are concrete. The specification should state the 2019 rule; both implementations keep what they do today, in a callout; one test marks the difference. Second, the crash I ranked first among the errors (row 447, the `fail` calls that fail JVM verification) has a designers' fix that is better than the one I recommended: the checker should never bind a type parameter to the empty type `Bottom`; it should bind it to the parameter's bound, or to the expected type. The paper says this outright. One small checker rung, and the same rung fixes rows 425 and 516. Third, the inference chapter batch N wrote says a type parameter with two unrelated arguments takes their union; the paper says that was an unproven guess and takes the bound; the implementations already do the latter; the text and two tests flip.
- Nothing changes in the big decisions. Route A, the flat tower, the overload sentence, the three rules, the conversion order, `comprises` on values and the implicit bound `Any` are all confirmed, the last one in so many words.
- Two things to know, no decision needed: the paper's soundness proof does not cover the library's own reductions (`SUM`, `BIG MAX`, the `Integral` family), because it forbids a bound that names the parameter itself; and the item 26 you approved is the one place our type theory goes past the designers' last proven model, since the paper keeps a unique static winner as a theorem where we keep it only at run time. Both go into the decision records as sentences.
- One thing for phase 5's list: the compiled dispatcher will need the call's static result type at run time, which the team's code generator never passed.

24	- A *witness* is an argument that carries a static argument and nothing else. The library has two: `__thrower[\T\]`, a function of type `() -> T` never called (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2372`), and `N[\n\]`, an object whose type carries a size (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NatReflect.fsi`).
25	- *Opening* a size is binding a size parameter to a number known only at run time, inside the code that runs with it. The type theory calls it unpacking an existential.
26	- A *bound* is the `extends` clause of a type parameter: `T extends Number` admits only number types for `T`.
27	- *The distance stage* is the gate's full checker measurement of the one library (`coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh`); its classes V1, V2 and Z1 are the array ones (`coordinator/tools/distance/classify.py:59-104`).
28	
29	## 1. What was measured for this note
30	
31	- The machine: 4 CPUs, Intel Xeon @ 2.10 GHz, OpenJDK 25.0.4, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, load 1 to 10 (other workers' runs; the VM restarted at 14:35 UTC and every run it cut was run again). Every capture's first lines name the load at its start. No timing below compares two runs; each width pair is taken in one JVM.
32	- The tree: `main` at `6bc21c364`. Nothing under `Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/` or `ProjectFortress/src/` has changed since `2770550c3` (batch N's rung M), so the batch N gate's distance table is today's (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-N/gate/distance.txt`, 627 errors; its sites `distance-sites.tsv`).
33	- The new measurements, each with its script and captures:
34	  - Decision D's diff re-based past climb batch 7's rename and checked on six copies (C4 as written, with the diff, their two split copies, the split copy beside the E3 library copy, and that copy with the powers written to one declaration), plus one with two planted errors; walk's check program on the patched copy. `reviews/decision-d-diff/rebase-2026-09-29/` (`run.sh`, `pow-variant.py`, `measure/`, `walk-threads1.txt`).
35	  - Four decision A probes, compiled and run in the compiler's own world and run under walk (`reviews/array-design-ways/probes/`, `run.sh`, `*.compile.txt`, `*.run.txt`, `*.walk.txt`).
36	  - Four library copies and an unchanged one through the gate's distance stage, each copy's sites compared with the unchanged one's (`reviews/array-design-ways/lib-variants.py`, `distance-copy.sh`, `sites-vs.py`, `captures/distance-*.table`, `captures/sites-*-vs-L0.txt`); the team's array tests under walk against five copies and an unchanged one (`walk-copy.sh`, `captures/walk-*.txt`); C4's check program under walk against one copy (`walk-c4-copy.sh`, `captures/walk-c4-STORE.txt`). The unchanged copy gives 625 errors where the gate gave 627, within the stage's stated run-to-run variation (`coordinator/tools/distance/run.sh`, its header); the big-operator class differs between any two runs at sites that name no array.
37	  - Two Java pairs for the element width, one JVM each (`probes/width/`).
38	
39	## 2. Question 1, decision D: the model's own sized types
40	
41	**The question.** C4's arrays are unsized in the model's own types, and the library's operators that the model applies to them are sized. On the compiled path, which checks the static types, the two meet at every such application. How do sizes enter the model's text?
42	
43	**The mathematics.** A shape is part of an operation's type: an m × n matrix times an n × p matrix is m × p, and a dot product takes two vectors of one length. A shape error is a type error, found without running anything.
44	
45	**What each path does today, measured today** (the re-based diff and its driver are `reviews/decision-d-diff/rebase-2026-09-29/`; captures under its `measure/`):
46	
47	- Walk dispatches on the run-time object. C4 builds its arrays with `array[\RR64\](n)`, whose objects are `Vector` and `Matrix` underneath (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2047`, `:2375-2379`), so C4 runs; its check program passes 40 of 40 (FACTS § The library's arrays and algebra, line 137).
48	- The compiled checker against the one library, C4 as written: 26 errors of C4's own (`measure/base.own.txt`).
49	  - 15 are decision D: the four row lifts, `plane` and the three `reflect` bridges in `FlatArrays`, `parseRow` twice in `FlatData`, `gather` twice and `DOT` three times in the model.
50	  - 5 are new since 2026-09-27: `10.0^(-5)` on the hyperparameter line (its second power, `10.0^(-8)`, is not reached), `10.0^10` in the mask, and the check program's three tolerances, each refused as an ambiguous coercion. `RR64`'s `^` on an `RR64` and `MultiplicativeRing`'s `^` on a `ZZ64` both apply only by converting the integer, and since batch N's rung I such a tie is refused (FACTS § The checker and the one library, line 79; `8dc1a74d9`). No ledger row names these sites; walk takes them.
51	  - 6 are the old small ones: `Character.codePoint`, `Diag`'s product body, the varargs `SUM` in `flat`, the varargs export, `matShape`'s body (row 474), `view`'s arity.
52	  - The 3 `fail[\T\]` errors of 2026-09-27 are gone (batch 7's rung B, `de22fd928`).
53	- The old counts were 24 before and 12 after (`reviews/decision-d-diff.md` § 5). Today's differ from them by those two changes on every copy:
54	  - C4 as written: 24 → 26.
55	  - With the diff: 12 → 14 (`measure/d.own.txt`). All 15 of decision D are gone as such; 3 `DOT`s fail on the library api's dead sizes (decision E's E3), 1 is the `adam` bridge, 1 is `numbersOf`'s discarded count, 5 are the powers, 4 are old small items.
56	  - The diagnostic copies, which write C4's three top-level tuple bindings as single bindings on the same lines (row 474's silent stop; not a model change): 25 → 28 before the diff, 15 → 18 after (`measure/base-split.own.txt`, `measure/d-split.own.txt`).
57	  - The split copy after the diff, beside a library copy without the 17 dead sizes (E3): 10 → 14 (`measure/d-split-e3.own.txt`). Here the powers do more than add errors. A refused power ends the check of its block, so `stepN` is now checked only to its mask line (`MicroGptFlat.fss:61` of the patched copy) and `adamN` to its update line (`:87`), where on 2026-09-27 the whole of `stepN` checked clean.
58	  - With the powers also written so that one declaration applies (a diagnostic copy, `rebase-2026-09-29/pow-variant.py`, not a model change): 7 (`measure/d-split-e3-pow.own.txt`). They are the old 10 less the three `fail` errors: the two bridges, `adamN`'s vector-plus-scalar division (row 475), `numbersOf`'s discarded count, the varargs `SUM` and export, `codePoint`. Two planted errors, one inside `rmsn_b` and one after `stepN`'s last statement, are both reported (`measure/d-split-e3-pow-plant.own.txt`), so the check reaches the end of the step: the forward and backward passes check clean at their sizes.
59	- Walk runs the patched C4: `MicroGptFlatCheck`, private cache, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, 40 PASS of 40 in 826 s at a load of 6 at the start, every line identical to `run-c4/checks/threads1.txt` once the timings are masked (`rebase-2026-09-29/walk-threads1.txt`). Not run: four threads.
60	
61	**The specification, under every spelling.**
62	
63	- The sized array type: "The type of a k-dimensional array expression is Array k[T, 0, n0, ..., 0, n(k-1)] ... This type can be abbreviated as T[n0, ..., n(k-1)]" (`Specification/basic/expressions/aggregate.tex:130-137`).
64	- The vector and matrix types, with sizes as exponents: "a vector of length n with element type T is written T^n" (`Specification/preliminaries/overview.tex:1075-1079`); `Matrix[T][n0 × ... × n(k-1)]`, abbreviated `T^(n0 × ... × n(k-1))`, in a margin note (`aggregate.tex:152-170`). Under walk `T^n` parses and denotes the library's `Number`-only `Vector` (row 24).
65	- A size in a signature: `makeVector`, "a nat parameter s0, which appears in both the parameter type and return type" (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:94-97`); a size "may be used ... in any context that a variable of type ℕ32 can appear" (`:83-86`).
66	- Two factories side by side: `array[E](size)` for "the specified runtime-determined size" and `array1[E,n]()` for "statically determined size n" (`Specification/advanced/parallelism-locality/arrays-distributed.tex:42-48`).
67	- A generic function named without its static arguments: "most identifier references do not include them; the static arguments are statically inferred from the context of the function call" (`Specification/basic/expressions/var-ref.tex:35-40`). The inference chapter as batch N's rung T wrote it leaves "an expected type in any context other than those listed above, such as an argument of another call" undescribed (`Specification/basic/inference.tex:201-205`).
68	
69	**The library's own practice.**
70	
71	- Sized results with shared sizes on every product: `opr DOT[\T extends Number, nat n, nat m, nat p\](me: Matrix[\T,n,m\], other: Matrix[\T,m,p\]): Matrix[\T,n,p\]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1701-1703`; FACTS line 131).
72	- An unsized public face for a size known only at run time, opened into a generic helper by `reflect`: `array[\E\](x:ZZ32):Array[\E,ZZ32\] = __arr1(__thrower[\E\],reflect(x))` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2047`, `:2055-2056`). Ledger row 25 calls this "the sanctioned escape".
73	- The sized factories `vector[\T,s0\]()`, `matrix[\T,s0,s1\]()`, `array3[\T,s0,s1,s2\]()` (`FortressLibrary.fsi:1578`, `:1688`; `FortressLibrary.fss:2955`).
74	- The focused APL base's `FlatArrays2` already declares the model's operations with their sizes (FACTS line 131).
75	
76	**The peers** (the record's survey, `reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md` § 6): C++, Rust and Chapel put sizes in types and make each instantiation its own code; Julia makes a size a type parameter and specialises per value at run time; Haskell carries type-level sizes and reflects a run-time number with `someNatVal`. Futhark writes sizes in function types and gives a function whose result length is known only at run time an existential size, "?[m].[m]t" (https://futhark.readthedocs.io/en/latest/language-reference.html, section 3.10.1).
77	
78	**The commits.** The team's library declared the sized traits and products and never checked them; the checker has checked sizes since climb batch 4's rung N (`3f297441c`), and the compiled run carries them since batch 5's rung Z (`e893a3e00`).
79	
80	**The ways.**
81	
82	1. **D1, sizes in the model's types through the library's own devices** (the re-based diff, `rebase-2026-09-29/decision-d.patch`). The model: 21 lines out, 29 in, the same lines as on 2026-09-27; no operator changes. The vocabulary: `FlatArrays.fsi` 30 lines out, 46 in; `FlatArrays.fss` 57 out, 65 in; `FlatData` 11 out, 12 in. The re-base changed only what climb batch 7's rename forced: 11 vocabulary lines now call `tabulate` and `tabulatedVector` where the old patch called `fill(f)` and the function form of `vector`, and one comment. What forces the model's 29 lines, by reading the diff (my reading):
83	   - 5 are the model's own functions with sized signatures: `rmsn`, `sm`, `rmsn_b`, `sm_b` and the `view` helper.
84	   - 2 are the local helpers `h` and `u`, sized and taking witnesses.
85	   - 10 open sizes known only at run time (question 4): the import of `NatReflect`, the two comment lines naming the sizes, the `step` bridge (2 lines) and `stepN`'s header (2), the `adam` bridge (1) and `adamN`'s header (2).
86	   - 5 write a size that no argument carries: `corpus.tokens[\R\]`, the nine `view[\V,E\]`, the two `onehot(…, N[\V\])` lines, and the mask moved into the step, whose size `T` is the step's parameter.
87	   - 7 write the size of a generic function passed to the row lift, `rows(rmsn[\E\], x)`. Both paths refuse a generic function as a value without it (row 156). The specification says such arguments are inferred from context (`var-ref.tex:35-40`), and its inference chapter does not yet describe that context (`inference.tex:201-205`). With that inference built, these 7 lines would stay as they are today (my reading).
88	2. **D2, the vocabulary over the unsized `Array`, the model unchanged.** The products the model uses (`DOT`, juxtaposition, `rows`, `gather`, `diag`) declared over `Array[\RR64,I\]` beside the library's sized ones. No model line changes. The checker then never sees a shape, and the sized products are not what the model runs: this is the sidestep his ruling of 2026-09-19 refuses ("I don't know [that] we can sidestep the nat issue", POSITIONS line 38).
89	3. **D3, the specification's own spelling of the same types.** D1 with `RR64^s` for `Vector[\RR64,s\]` and `RR64^(r × c)` for `Matrix[\RR64,r,c\]` (`overview.tex:1078`, `aggregate.tex:152-170`). The same lines change; they read shorter. Measured on a six-line program (`reviews/array-design-ways/probes/pow/TPow.fss`): the compiled checker against the one library stops the component, "Desugaring MatrixType at TPow.fss:7.19 to TraitType is not yet supported" (`TPow.check.txt`); walk parses the signature and fails at the call, "Cannot unify __DefaultVector[\RR64,3\] ... with MatrixType" (`TPow.walk.txt`). Neither path takes the spelling today; it needs the type `T^n` desugared to `Vector[\T,n\]` on both.
90	4. **D4, sizes static from the top** (my reading, not measured). Every size of the step is a literal somewhere up the call chain if the batch size is a static choice: the check program calls the step at batch 1 and batch 4. The step then takes its sizes as static parameters from its callers, and the `reflect` bridges go; the model's api `MicroGptFlat.fsi` and the check program's calls change instead. It fixes the batch size at compile time.
91	
92	**What each costs.**
93	
94	- D1 changes 29 model lines, each shown to him as a diff (POSITIONS 2026-09-19). What is left for the model's gate after it, measured: the api's 17 dead sizes (decision E's E3; the regenerated patch `rebase-2026-09-29/library-e3.patch` applies to today's tree), a rule to open a run-time size (question 4), the powers' tie, the tuple-binding defect (row 474), the vector-plus-scalar `+` (row 475), the `Character` crash (row 477), and four small items.
95	- D2 changes no model line and gives up the checked shapes.
96	- D3 is D1 with the specification's notation, and first the desugaring of `T^n` on both paths.
97	- D4 moves the change from the model's step into its api and caller, and removes the run-time sizes the step opens.
98	
99	## 3. Question 2, decision A: what puts `double[]` under the library's generic array traits
100	
101	**The question.** His decision of 2026-09-19 makes the store a JVM `double[]`, and the library's arrays are generic in their element type: `Vector[\T, nat s0\]` keeps its elements in `mem: PrimitiveArray[\T,s0\]` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fss:2339-2345`). What makes a `Vector[\RR64, 16\]` hold a `double[]` while a `Vector[\T, 16\]` of another `T` keeps a boxed store?
102	
103	**The mathematics.** None: the choice changes how the numbers are held, not what they mean.
104	
105	**What each path does today.**
106	
107	- Walk: every store is `PrimitiveArray`, boxed values in an `AtomicArray` (`coordinator/array-design.md` § 1). The team wrote one unboxed store: `object PrimImmutableRR64Array[\nat s0\]() extends ImmutableArray1[\RR64,0,s0\]` over a Java `double[]` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fss:43-52`; `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/interpreter/glue/prim/PrimImmutableRR64Array.java`). Jan Maessen, 2008-07-28: "Immutable arrays of unboxed RR64. When you request an immutable array of RR64 these should be used in preference to the boxed version" (`353818213`). No library file names it; nothing selects it.
108	- The compiled path: stamping renames classes and cannot produce a `double[]` field (`coordinator/array-design.md` § 2, probe 1). The only unboxed stores are two hand-written Java classes, `FZZ32Vector` over an `int[]` and `FStringVector`, lowered straight to their classes by a table in the code generator; every element read is boxed through seven frames; a native helper cannot take a Java array (FACTS § The territory map, line 160).
109	- What an unboxed store buys alone, measured on 2026-09-20: nothing. The dot product over a `double[]` read and written through a boxing accessor is 8.9 times primitive, against 6.4 times for boxed storage; the matrix product 6.6 against 6.2 (`reviews/array-design-review.md`, Serious 4; `compiler-probes/array-design-review/java-medians.tsv`). The traffic is unboxed only by decision B, phase 6 (PLAN.md).
110	- The library's selection device, measured here on both paths (`reviews/array-design-ways/probes/`, one private cache per path; the compiled path in the compiler's own world, since the switch-over has not happened):
111	  - `WayANoCast.fss`: a generic factory with the library's witness `typecase` (`array1`'s, `FortressLibrary.fss:2375-2379`) whose `RR64` arm returns a store written for `RR64` alone. The checker refuses it, "Function body has type OR(DStore,BStore[\T\]), but declared return type is Arr[\T\]", as on 2026-09-20; walk runs it and picks `DStore` for `RR64`.
112	  - `WayACast.fss`: the same arm through the library's `cast`, `cast[\Arr[\T\]\](DStore(...))`, the device of `additiveIdentity` (`FortressLibrary.fss:3140-3155`). The checker accepts it. The compiled run and walk both print `RR64 DStore 1.5` and `ZZ32 BStore 7`.
113	  - `WayACastSized.fss`: the same with sizes, `vec[\T, nat n\]` returning `cast[\Vec[\T,n\]\](DVec[\n\](...))`. Accepted; both paths pick `DVec[\16\]` for `RR64` and the generic store for `ZZ32`, and a function with a shared size takes two of them.
114	  - `WayASpec.fss`: specialisation by overloading, a plain `mk(w: () -> RR64, x: RR64)` beside the generic `mk[\T\](w: () -> T, x: T)`, called from generic code with the library's witness. The checker accepts it and the compiled run dispatches to the plain declaration for `RR64` and to the generic one for `ZZ32`. Walk refuses the pair when it loads the program, "has a parameter with generic type, at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types", its declaration-time family check (rows 159 and 475).
115	
116	**The specification.**
117	
118	- "Fortress arrays are complex data structures; simple linear storage is encapsulated by the HeapSequence type, which is used in the implementation of arrays" (`Specification/advanced/parallelism-locality/arrays-distributed.tex:18-22`), marked not yet supported (`:15-16`).
119	- Jan Maessen's note on unboxed types, recorded in the draft: "Do we want to permit arrays of fixed bounds to be unboxed? No. Unboxed arrays are a different other thing. Among other things, an array of fixed bounds may be a segment of another array" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:42`). The sized array is a structure; the linear store under it is what is unboxed.
120	- Jan's own example of the selection, in the draft's future work on overloading by static parameters: `array1[\T extends Object, nat s0\]()` beside `array1[\T extends Number, nat s0\](): Vector[\T,s0\]` (`future.tex:236-246`). The library's `array1` does it with the witness `typecase` meanwhile, "TODO: fix when Number is covariant" (`FortressLibrary.fss:2374`).

6. **6f, arithmetic declared on `Number`.** `opr +(self, other: Number): Number` loses `T`, and route A removed `Number`'s arithmetic by design (FACTS line 116); refused by the flat tower (my reading).

**What each costs.** 6a costs nothing and keeps 36 errors. 6b is three library lines. 6c is 61 library lines; measured, it trades V1's 36 errors for 8 new ones with `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]` alone, and for 1 new site with the two-trait bound (the two factory sites then reported once per bound), which keeps `Number`'s exclusions and makes the checker's overloading stage several times slower on the library. 6d restructures the traits and their products and touches row 299's override. 6e waits for `where` clauses. 6f undoes route A.

## 8. The forks for Pavol, in the order they need deciding

The order follows what each answer unblocks (my reading of `coordinator/PLAN.md`): the first three sit on phase 3's road to the checker's true zero, which batch 8 drives class by class after batch 7b; the width fixes the types the model's diff writes; the model's diff opens with the run-time sizes it needs; the mechanism comes with the speed of phase 6. Each is one question with its ways; none is recommended here.

1. **Arithmetic in a size (item 15).** How does the library keep its rank-2 and rank-3 storage, whose field is sized by a product? Ways: 15a the checker compares size expressions by structure and folds numerals (the default on record, batch 8 or later); 15b the library makes the field at run time with its own `primitiveArray` (three lines; measured: the 8 storage errors go, none is new, walk and C4's check unchanged; on the compiled path it needs question 4's answer); 15c full static arithmetic; 15d a native store per rank. It holds 11 of the distance stage's errors and `reflect`'s own body.
2. **The bound of `Vector` and `Matrix` (question 6).** What gives their bodies arithmetic? Ways: 6a `Number` as landed; 6c the library's `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]` (measured: alone it clears V1's 36 and brings 8 new errors where `Number`'s closure was doing work; beside `Number` in the library's two-trait form it clears 34 and brings 1, and the checker's overloading stage runs several times longer); 6d a bound per operation, moving the products out of the traits; 6e the specification's algebra, after `where` clauses; 6f arithmetic on `Number`, against route A. 6b, the storing objects taking their traits' bound, is a slip under every way. It holds 36 of the distance stage's errors.
3. **A size known only at run time (question 4).** How does a number become a size the checker accepts and the compiled path runs? Ways: 4a the library's `reflect` with the checker taught the team's commented rule; 4b `reflect` built in over design B's factory, with 4a's rule; 4c run-time sizes stay unsized; 4d no run-time sizes in the step; 4e a `typecase` that binds a size, after `where` clauses. It holds the library's own `array[\E\](x)` (six of V2's errors) and decision D's two bridges.
4. **The element width (question 5).** `RR64` or `RR32`? Ways: 5a `RR64` as written; 5b `RR32` throughout, with new float32 goldens from the reference and rung V first; 5c the model generic in its width; 5d the width named once by a type alias, after aliases are built; 5e `RR32` storage with `RR64` sums, the draft's `Extended`. Every type line of decision D's diff and every store of decision A follows from it.
5. **The model's sized types (decision D).** How do sizes enter the model's text? Ways: D1 the re-based diff, 21 model lines out and 29 in; D2 the vocabulary over the unsized `Array`, the model unchanged and its shapes unchecked; D3 D1 in the specification's `T^n` notation, which neither path takes today; D4 sizes static from the top, the batch size fixed at compile time. D1's 10 bridge lines are question 4's answer, and its 7 `rows(rmsn[\E\], …)` lines are the inference of a generic function passed as an argument, which the specification promises and its inference chapter does not yet describe.
6. **What puts `double[]` under the generic traits (decision A).** Ways: A1 the library's witness `typecase` with its `cast` (measured on both paths); A2 a plain factory beside the generic one (compiled yes, walk refuses the pair today); A3 a factory name per element type; A4 the loader stamps an `RR64` class, the team's `Unbox` direction; A5 a special type, as `ZZ32Vector`. None is faster alone; decision B (phase 6) unboxes the traffic.

## 9. Found on the way

- **The model's numeral powers are refused by the compiled checker since climb batch N's rung I.** `10.0^(-5)`, `10.0^(-8)`, `-(10.0^10)` and the check program's three tolerances meet `RR64`'s `^` on an `RR64` and `MultiplicativeRing[\RR64\]`'s `^` on a `ZZ64`, both only by converting the integer; the tie is refused, and the refusal ends the check of its block (`rebase-2026-09-29/measure/base.own.txt`, `d.own.txt`, `d-split-e3.own.txt`). Walk takes them. No ledger row names it; the declarations are `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:278` and `:358`.
- **The comment that decision D's note of 2026-09-27 called the library's own is the revival's.** "sized arrays under a compiler need per-shape declarations beside these" was written by the revival on 2026-09-23 (`c2b4e2c95`) and reworded on 2026-09-28 (`581356f32`); today it reads "a static checker sees only Array[\T,I\], so the rank and size of a sized argument are lost to it in the result" (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2595-2600`). The team's own statement on per-type storage is Maessen's commit message of 2008 (section 3).
- **A two-trait bound on the array traits makes the compiled checker's Meet Rule check of the library several times slower.** With `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }` on `Vector` and `Matrix`, `FortressLibrary` took 3,825 s against 704 s unchanged, most of it in the component's overloading stage, in nested exclusion tests through the `comprises` check (section 7; `captures/distance-RINGNUM-stack.txt`). Not a pair of one run; batch 8's Meet Rule work (class M1, 109 errors) runs in the same code.
- **Decision E's patch applies again.** `rebase-2026-09-29/library-e3.patch` is the 17 dead sizes regenerated on today's library; `git apply --check` passes.

## 10. What is measured, what is read, what was not run

- **Measured here:** the re-based diff on seven checker copies and under walk (section 2); the four decision A probes on both paths (section 3); four library copies and an unchanged one through the distance stage, the team's array tests under walk against five copies, and C4's check program against one (sections 4 and 7); D3's `T^n` on both paths (section 2); the two width pairs (section 6).
- **Cited from the record, not re-run:** the batch N gate's distance table and sites, today's tree (V1, V2, Z1); the boxing costs of `perf-probes/kernels/` and `reviews/array-design-review.md`; the design B size machinery (FACTS lines 42, 43, 114); the peers' survey of `reviews/size-runtime-design-brief.md` § 6 and `reviews/nat-checking-plan.md` § g.
- **Read, not measured:** the checker rules of 15a and 4a and what they would clear; 4b, A4 and A5, which need `.java` work; D4; 5c, 5d, 5e; 6d; the costs marked "my reading".
- **Not run:** the gate (nothing tracked outside this note's directories changed); the four-thread check; the compiled path for C4 beyond the checker; the APL program's twin of the diff (`apl/mg/FlatArrays2`).

(p. 11:21).

## 5. The run-time check on the return type

- **What it is.** Every call carries its static return type into run time
  (§5.1, p. 11:16). Dispatch uses it as an upper bound when it instantiates
  the chosen declaration (p. 11:18).
- **It never moves a call to another declaration.**
  - Lemma 5.8: whatever instance the checker chose, "there exists a
    type-safe most specific method instance at run time" (p. 11:22). Its proof
    is where [Return-Test] is used (pp. 11:22-23).
  - Lemma 5.9: the first-dispatchable scan then yields an instance of the
    most specific declaration applicable to the ilks, with a return type below
    the static one (p. 11:23).
  - In a well-formed program the return-type bounds therefore never rule out
    that declaration. They only choose its instance.
- **What it costs.**
  - "In simple invariant cases, we expect the run-time cost to be relatively
    low but nonzero", since matching `List⟦String⟧` against `List⟦T⟧` only
    binds T (pp. 11:24-25).
  - For the covariant and contravariant cases, "caching or dynamic
    recompilation … may help" (p. 11:25).
  - The discussion calls left-to-right scoping "a relatively small sacrifice
    of expressivity for a large gain in dynamic efficiency" (p. 11:24).

## 6. What it proves and what it leaves open

**Proved (sketched here, full proofs in the companion report):**
- Theorem 4.1: a unique most specific declaration exists (p. 11:15).
- Soundness and completeness of type matching and of solving (Lemmas 5.1 to
  5.4), and so of the dispatch semipredicate (Theorems 5.5, 5.6;
  pp. 11:21-22). Completeness of matching assumes that a matched type holds
  no `Bottom` and no type parameter inside a union or intersection. The
  paper shows that every use meets this: declared types have neither, and
  unions reach a declaration only through already-ground instances
  (pp. 11:21-22).
- Lemmas 5.7 to 5.9 (pp. 11:22-23).
- Theorem 5.10, soundness of a method call: a well-typed call is reduced by
  [R-Method] and its body's type is below the call's static type (p. 11:23).
- Theorem 5.11, type soundness: if `e` types to `(ϵ, д)` and `ϵ` evaluates to
  a value, the value's type is below `д` (p. 11:24).
  He adds a second, cross-instantiation restriction between a covariant
  subtrait and its supertrait (`:540-566`). He finds that the numeric tower's
  self-type idiom breaks it, and that "more work needs to be done"
  (`:568-633`). His suggested rewrite puts the self type in a bound,
  `add⟦X <: Ring⟦X⟧⟧(X, X): X` (`:620-624`).

**Naden, "Enforcing Fortress' Return Type Rule at Runtime"** (2012-08-31,
`Papers/RuntimeInstantiation/RTRinstantionTheory.tex`, with the notes of
May to July 2012 beside it).
- *Proposed:* adding bounds from the call's static return type to run-time
  instantiation "without changing which function definition will be chosen"
  (`:73-80`).
- *Proved:* a theorem that under the Return Type Rule the return-type bounds
  are satisfiable exactly when applicability is, so they can join the
  single pass (`:279-298`).
- *Not done:* the bound-generation algorithm and the open coding (`:84-89`).

**POPL 2019 against these.**
- It carries out the second write-up in a full calculus, with proofs: the
  return-type bounds in the semipredicate, and Lemmas 5.8 and 5.9.
- It stays within the first write-up's position: overload sets are validated
  statically and without context, the Return Type Rule is kept, and the
  exclusion rule is kept with the covariant relaxation, extended to
  contravariance.
- It does not do what that write-up rejected: the static type chooses the
  instance, never the declaration (§5 above). One part of Naden's objection
  still applies to the instance: which instance runs depends on static
  information (the `append` example).
- It has no counterpart to the cross-instantiation restriction. Whether
  [Return-Test] refuses Naden's `coTail` pair instead has not been worked
  out here.
  covers every instance of the less specific declaration (p. 11:15), and
  its universal reduction is the paper's form of "except where the domain
  reduction forces an equality" (pp. 11:14-15). The rung can cite Fig. 5 and

- **Run-time instantiation of a dispatched generic (item 30, POSITIONS
  2026-09-29).** The decision: the generic declaration runs, at the instance
  the value fixes, and at the least instance within the bounds where it fixes
  none; Naden's return-type restriction is future work
  (`reviews/plain-beside-generic-judgement.md:74`, `:159`).

content.content:
Now we describe how to determine which coercion is applied to a given
call in terms of rewriting functional calls.  The rewriting is
for pedagogical purposes; implementation techniques may vary.

Consider a static call $\f(\As)$ or $\As_0.\f(\As)$.  Let $\Sigma$ be
the set of parameter types of functional declarations of $\f$ that are
applicable to the call.
Let $\Sigma'$ be the set of parameter types of
functional declarations of $\f$ that are
applicable with coercion to the call.
If $\Sigma$ is not empty then we use the overloading resolution
described in \secref{resolving-overloading} to determine which
element of $\Sigma$ is called.
If $\Sigma$ is empty but $\Sigma'$ is not, then we rewrite the call as
follows.  Define: \[\mathpzc{C} = \{T \in \Sigma' \mid S \coercedefto T
\logicand \As \Ovrsubtype S\}.\] Let $T \in \mathpzc{C}$ be the most
specific element of $\mathpzc{C}$.  In other words, there does not exist
$T' \in \mathpzc{C}$ such that $T' \morespecific T$.  The restrictions
given in \secref{restrictions-coercion} and
\chapref{overloaded-declarations} guarantee that such a $T$
exists and that it is unique.  The call $\f(\As)$ or $\As_0.\f(\As)$ is
rewritten to \EXP{f(\mathrm{coercion}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(\TYP{A}))} or
\EXP{A_{0}.f(\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(A))}
and the declaration with parameter
type $T$ is applied to the call.

As an example, consider the following definitions:
